name: Antipas (martyr in Pergamum)
title: Christ's Faithful Witness in Pergamum
summary: Antipas is the only Christian martyr mentioned by name in Revelation. In the letter to the church in Pergamum, Jesus honors him with the title "my faithful witness" – a designation otherwise reserved for Jesus himself. Antipas met his death in Pergamum, a city marked by intense pagan worship and emperor cult, which Jesus describes as the place "where Satan has his throne". Through his uncompromising faithfulness amid a hostile religious environment, Antipas became an example for the early church. His martyrdom illustrates the high price the first Christians paid for their confession, and Jesus' recognition of him underscores that faithfulness unto death holds eternal value in God's kingdom.
roles: leader of the church in Pergamum (according to tradition)

keyEvents.title: Honored by Jesus as a Faithful Witness
keyEvents.description: In the letter to the church in Pergamum, Jesus refers to Antipas as "my faithful witness" (Greek: ὁ μάρτυς μου ὁ πιστός). This title reflects Jesus' own title in Rev 1:5 and marks an exceptional honor given to a named believer in Scripture.

keyEvents.title: Martyrdom in Pergamum
keyEvents.description: Antipas was killed for his faith in Pergamum, a city Jesus describes as the place "where Satan has his throne." The city was a center of emperor worship, Zeus cult, and the cult of Asclepius, so Christian confession meant direct confrontation with powerful religious and political forces.

keyEvents.title: Context: The Letter to the Church in Pergamum
keyEvents.description: In the letter to Pergamum, Jesus acknowledges the church's faithfulness and Antipas' sacrifice but rebukes them for tolerating followers of Balaam's teaching and the Nicolaitans, who encouraged idolatry and immorality. Antipas' unwavering loyalty stands in sharp contrast to the compromise threatening the church.

versions.summary: Antipas was a Christian martyr in Pergamum mentioned by Jesus himself in the Book of Revelation. He is described as Christ's faithful witness who was killed for his faith in a city that was a center of idol worship. His martyrdom stands as an early example of the persecution faced by the first Christians.
versions.title: The Faithful Witness
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Faithful Witness' is good and based directly on Rev 2:13, but it could be refined to 'Christ's Faithful Witness in Pergamum' to provide more context and distinguish from others who might be called faithful witnesses.; [minor] The role 'martyr' is correct, but one might consider adding 'faithful witness' as a role, since this is the specific term Jesus uses for Antipas.; [minor] The description states that Jesus uses Antipas as an example and 'encourages them to hold fast to the faith.' However, the context in Rev 2:12-17 is somewhat more complex: Jesus commends the church's faithfulness but also rebukes them for tolerating false teaching (the Nicolaitans and the teaching of Balaam). Verse 14 concerns rebuke, not encouragement. The reference should be adjusted.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. There are rich historical, linguistic, and theological details about Antipas and Pergamum that should be covered: the Greek word 'martys' (witness/martyr), Pergamum's religious context with the altar of Zeus and the cult of Asclepius, as well as later church traditions regarding Antipas's method of death.

versions.summary: Antipas was a Christian martyr in Pergamum mentioned by Jesus himself in the book of Revelation. He is called "my faithful witness" – the same title that Jesus bears himself – and was killed for his faith in a city that was a prominent center of idol worship and emperor cult. The expression "where Satan has his throne" testifies to Pergamum's role as a religious power center. Antipas' martyrdom stands as an early and moving example of the persecution the first Christians faced, and his faithfulness unto death is held up by Christ himself as exemplary.
versions.title: Christ's Faithful Witness in Pergamum
versions.reason: [minor] The Greek rendering "ho martys mou ho pistos mou" is imprecise. The Greek text in Rev 2:13 reads ὁ μάρτυς μου ὁ πιστός μου, but the most common critical reading has only ὁ μάρτυς μου ὁ πιστός (without the second μου). The double μου appears in some manuscripts but should be clarified.; [minor] The summary is well phrased but closely resembles the previous version (v1). Since stricter evaluation against one prior version is required, the text should be rephrased more distinctly to avoid repetition and add new nuances.; [minor] The role "faithful witness" can be supplemented with "Christian leader in Pergamum," based on the honor Jesus gives him, even though we do not know his exact function in the congregation.

footnotes.text: The Greek word μάρτυς (martys), used of Antipas in Rev 2:13, originally means 'witness.' Over time, the word came to mean 'martyr' precisely because so many early Christian witnesses paid with their lives for their testimony. Antipas is one of the earliest named persons in the New Testament where this double meaning is clear.

Pergamum was known as a major religious center in antiquity. The city housed the monumental Altar of Zeus, a large temple for emperor worship (the Temple of Augustus), and the sanctuary of the healing god Asclepius, whose symbol was the serpent. The expression 'where Satan has his throne' in Rev 2:13 may allude to one or more of these cult centers.

According to later church traditions, including martyr acts from the Byzantine period, Antipas is said to have been bishop of Pergamum and burned alive inside a bronze bull during the reign of Emperor Domitian (c. 81–96 AD). These traditions are late and cannot be verified from the Bible, but they reflect the early church's reverence for Antipas.

The title 'my faithful witness' (ὁ μάρτυς μου ὁ πιστός) that Jesus gives to Antipas in Rev 2:13 is remarkable because it mirrors the title Jesus himself bears in Rev 1:5 (ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστός – 'the faithful witness'). This parallel suggests that Antipas, in his martyrdom, followed his Lord's example of faithfulness.

Pergamum was also home to a famous library that rivaled the library of Alexandria in antiquity. The word 'parchment' derives from the city's name, as this writing material was developed there as an alternative to papyrus.

The name Ἀντίπας (Antipas) is likely a short form of Ἀντίπατρος (Antipater), meaning 'in place of the father' or 'against all.' The same name was borne by Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee, but he is a completely different person. That a Christian in a Hellenistic city bore a Greek name was very common in the early congregations of Asia Minor.
